name: The Vagrant
description:
The Vagrant is a city that refuses to stay put. A mobile seacrete-and-steel platform approximately 800 meters long and 400 meters wide, the Vagrant moves between the Great Lakes via the canal and lock systems that connect them — the Welland Canal between Erie and Ontario, the Soo Locks between Huron and Superior, the Straits of Mackinac between Huron and Michigan, and the Chicago Sanitary Canal connecting Michigan to the Mississippi watershed (though the Vagrant has only used this route twice, both times under circumstances its captain describes as 'interesting'). It is, depending on your perspective, a nomadic free city, a floating trade bazaar, a diplomatic headache, or the most creative interpretation of maritime law since someone first nailed a flag to a boat.

The Vagrant started as a conventional barge platform — a decommissioned Great Lakes ore carrier called the SS Edmund Reborn (the name was deliberate and nobody aboard apologizes for it) — purchased in 2176 by a collective of traders, smugglers, and maritime engineers who wanted access to every lake city without belonging to any of them. Over two decades, the original hull has been expanded, reinforced, and encrusted with seacrete growth that the collective encourages along the waterline and hull, creating an organic armor layer that makes the Vagrant look like a ship that a reef is slowly eating. Which is accurate. The seacrete accretion is continuous — every lake the Vagrant visits adds minerals to its hull in different chemical signatures, and marine geologists can read the Vagrant's travel history in cross-sections of its encrustation the way dendrochronologists read tree rings.

The Vagrant's legal status is its masterpiece. Because it moves between lakes, it is simultaneously in and out of every jurisdiction. When it's on Lake Michigan, it's outside M88's territorial waters. When it's on Erie, Cormorant Naval Systems classifies it as a 'transient vessel.' When it's on Ontario, the remnant Canadian government lists it as an 'unincorporated maritime entity.' The Vagrant's captain — elected by the resident population every three years, currently a former Cormorant Naval Systems deserter named Idris Achebe — maintains that the Vagrant is a sovereign vessel under maritime common law and that its residents are citizens of the Vagrant and nowhere else. Every legal authority on the Great Lakes has a different opinion about this claim's validity. None of them can agree on whose jurisdiction it falls under, which is exactly the point.

The Vagrant serves as a mobile marketplace, connecting the lake cities' economies in ways that fixed trade routes cannot. It carries goods, passengers, mail, and information between all seven settlements, plus shore communities that the corponations would prefer remained unconnected. It is the circulatory system of the free lake city network — the moving platform that turns isolated settlements into a connected civilization. Population: 12,000 permanent residents, plus a transient population of traders, passengers, and stowaways that varies between 3,000 and 8,000 depending on the season and which lake the Vagrant is currently on.

sights: A massive barge-platform encrusted in multi-colored seacrete layers — each lake's mineral signature visible in the hull like geological strata
Market stalls lining the main deck, their goods changing completely depending on which lake the Vagrant is currently transiting
The navigation tower — the original Edmund Reborn's bridge, now elevated on seacrete-grown pylons, flying the Vagrant's flag (a compass rose on black)
Docking clamps and gangway systems designed to interface with every lake city's unique harbor architecture
The wake — the Vagrant displaces enough water that its passage is visible from shore, a moving V-shape that announces its arrival hours before docking
sounds: Engines — the Vagrant runs on a hybrid system of converted diesel, wave energy, and a single Charnel Propulsion plasma-electric drive (acquired through channels the captain declines to discuss)
Trade — the constant negotiation of a floating bazaar, in every language spoken on the Great Lakes
The hull groaning as seacrete layers shift with temperature changes between lakes — the Vagrant complains audibly about weather
Lock mechanisms when transiting canals — the grinding, rushing, mechanical symphony of water levels changing
smells: Every lake simultaneously — the Vagrant carries the mineral signatures of all five Great Lakes in its seacrete layers, and they off-gas differently in different temperatures
Market goods — whatever's being traded this week, from Shallowgrave algae compounds to Deepwell ore samples to Tidebreak artwork
Engine exhaust from the hybrid drive system — cleaner than diesel, dirtier than plasma, distinctively Vagrant
The particular smell of a ship that has been lived on continuously for twenty-five years and has developed its own microbiome
atmosphere.feel: Freedom as a vehicle. The Vagrant feels like what it is — a city that decided the best way to avoid being controlled was to never stop moving. There's an energy aboard that's different from any fixed settlement: the transience, the constant change of scenery and trading partners, the knowledge that tomorrow you'll be on a different lake surrounded by different water. It's exciting and unstable in equal measure. The permanent residents have a particular looseness — people who've chosen motion over roots, who define home as a heading rather than a location. The Vagrant doesn't belong anywhere. That's the whole idea.

demographics: 12,000 permanent residents, plus 3,000-8,000 transient population. Permanent residents are a self-selected community of traders, mechanics, sailors, and people who cannot or will not stay in one place. Demographically diverse — the Vagrant draws from every lake city and every shore community. Children born aboard are 'wave-born' — citizens of the Vagrant from birth, which means citizens of nowhere that any shore-based authority recognizes.
economy: Trade arbitrage — buying where goods are cheap and selling where they're expensive, which is the oldest economic model and still the most effective. The Vagrant's mobility gives it access to every market on the Great Lakes, and its cargo holds are a rotating inventory of whatever the lake cities need from each other. Annual trade volume: approximately Φ5.7 billion, most of it in physical goods that can't be transmitted digitally. The Vagrant charges transit fees, docking fees, and a percentage on all transactions conducted aboard. Captain Achebe calls this 'the motion tax.' The residents call it rent.
power_structure: The Captain — elected every three years by permanent residents — holds executive authority over navigation, defense, and external relations. A Ship's Council of eight elected members manages internal affairs, trade regulation, and dispute resolution. The Vagrant's security force, the Hull Watch, is a volunteer militia of 600 armed residents trained in shipboard combat and canal defense. Governance is pragmatic: the Captain decides where the ship goes, the Council decides what happens aboard, and the residents decide both by vote when they disagree strongly enough.
dangers: Canal transit — the Vagrant is large enough that lock passage is a complex, vulnerable operation. Ambush during canal transit is the city's nightmare scenario.
Jurisdictional hostility — every authority on the Great Lakes has a reason to impound the Vagrant. None can agree on who has the right to, which is protection, but it's not permanent.
Mechanical failure — the Vagrant is a twenty-five-year-old converted ore carrier. Things break.
Smuggling — the Vagrant's cargo holds contain legitimate trade and things that are very much not. The line between the two is the Captain's judgment call.
Weather — a mobile platform cannot anchor and hunker like a fixed city. The Vagrant must navigate storms, not endure them.
opportunities: Access to every lake city market — the Vagrant is the only entity that trades with all seven settlements
Information flow — the Vagrant carries news, intelligence, and rumors between isolated communities
Jurisdictional immunity — the Vagrant's legal ambiguity protects people and goods that need protecting
The Captain's network — Idris Achebe knows everyone on the Great Lakes, and everyone knows him. His introductions open doors.
story_hooks: The Vagrant is transiting the Welland Canal when Cormorant Naval Systems attempts to board, citing a new sovereignty enforcement order. Captain Achebe needs someone on shore to challenge the order's legality before the Hull Watch has to fight.
A sealed cargo container loaded at Tidebreak turns out to contain something alive. The Vagrant is mid-lake with no port for 200 kilometers, and the container is making sounds.

Kyle needs to get from Meridian 88 to a lake city without any corponation knowing. The Vagrant is his only option — but passage requires a favor that the Captain will collect at the worst possible time.

adjacent_to: Currently varies — the Vagrant's connections change with its position
All five Great Lakes (accessible via canal systems)
All seven lake city settlements (regular trade partner)
Shore communities along the canal routes (informal trade relationships)
Meridian 88 (via Lake Michigan approach — the Vagrant docks at independent piers outside Cormorant's patrols)

frequented_by: Traders from every lake city and most shore communities
Passengers transiting between settlements without fixed schedules
Information couriers who use the Vagrant's mobility to move data physically
People who need to disappear — the Vagrant's constant motion makes tracking difficult
